L103: The Claude Developer Platform provides regex-based and BM25-based search tools out of the box, but you can also implement custom search tools using embeddings or other strategies.
L104: ### When to use the Tool Search Tool
L105: 
L106: Like any architectural decision, enabling the Tool Search Tool involves trade-offs. The feature adds a search step before tool invocation, so it delivers the best ROI when the context savings and accuracy improvements outweigh additional latency.
L107: 
L108: Use it when:
L109: 
L110:   * Tool definitions consuming >10K tokens
L111:   * Experiencing tool selection accuracy issues
L112:   * Building MCP-powered systems with multiple servers
L113:   * 10+ tools available
L114: 
L115: Less beneficial when:
L116:   * Small tool library (<10 tools)
L117:   * All tools used frequently in every session
L118:   * Tool definitions are compact
L119: ## Programmatic Tool Calling
L120: ### The challenge
L121: 
L122: Traditional tool calling creates two fundamental problems as workflows become more complex:
L123:   * Context pollution from intermediate results: When Claude analyzes a 10MB log file for error patterns, the entire file enters its context window, even though Claude only needs a summary of error frequencies. When fetching customer data across multiple tables, every record accumulates in context regardless of relevance. These intermediate results consume massive token budgets and can push important information out of the context window entirely.
L124:   * Inference overhead and manual synthesis: Each tool call requires a full model inference pass. After receiving results, Claude must "eyeball" the data to extract relevant information, reason about how pieces fit together, and decide what to do next—all through natural language processing. A five tool workflow means five inference passes plus Claude parsing each result, comparing values, and synthesizing conclusions. This is both slow and error-prone.
L125: ### Our solution
L126: 
L127: Programmatic Tool Calling enables Claude to orchestrate tools through code rather than through individual API round-trips. Instead of Claude requesting tools one at a time with each result being returned to its context, Claude writes code that calls multiple tools, processes their outputs, and controls what information actually enters its context window.
L128: Claude excels at writing code and by letting it express orchestration logic in Python rather than through natural language tool invocations, you get more reliable, precise control flow. Loops, conditionals, data transformations, and error handling are all explicit in code rather than implicit in Claude's reasoning.
L129: #### Example: Budget compliance check
L130: 
L131: Consider a common business task: "Which team members exceeded their Q3 travel budget?"
L132: 
L133: You have three tools available:
L134: 
L135:   * `get_team_members(department)` - Returns team member list with IDs and levels
L136:   * `get_expenses(user_id, quarter)` - Returns expense line items for a user
L137:   * `get_budget_by_level(level)` - Returns budget limits for an employee level
L138: 
L139: Traditional approach:
L140:   * Fetch team members → 20 people
L141:   * For each person, fetch their Q3 expenses → 20 tool calls, each returning 50-100 line items (flights, hotels, meals, receipts)
L142:   * Fetch budget limits by employee level
L143:   * All of this enters Claude's context: 2,000+ expense line items (50 KB+)
L144:   * Claude manually sums each person's expenses, looks up their budget, compares expenses against budget limits
L145:   * More round-trips to the model, significant context consumption
L146: 
L147: With Programmatic Tool Calling:
L148: Instead of each tool result returning to Claude, Claude writes a Python script that orchestrates the entire workflow. The script runs in the Code Execution tool (a sandboxed environment), pausing when it needs results from your tools. When you return tool results via the API, they're processed by the script rather than consumed by the model. The script continues executing, and Claude only sees the final output.
L149: cite11†Image: Programmatic tool calling flow Programmatic Tool Calling enables Claude to orchestrate tools through code rather than through individual API round-trips, allowing for parallel tool execution.
L150: Here's what Claude's orchestration code looks like for the budget compliance task:
L151: 
L152:     `team = await get_team_members("engineering")
L153: 
L154:     # Fetch budgets for each unique level
L155:     levels = list(set(m["level"] for m in team))
L156:     budget_results = await asyncio.gather(*[
L157:         get_budget_by_level(level) for level in levels
L158:     ])
L159: 
L160:     # Create a lookup dictionary: {"junior": budget1, "senior": budget2, ...}
L161:     budgets = {level: budget for level, budget in zip(levels, budget_results)}
L162:     # Fetch all expenses in parallel
L163:     expenses = await asyncio.gather(*[
L164:         get_expenses(m["id"], "Q3") for m in team
L165:     ])
L166: 
L167:     # Find employees who exceeded their travel budget
L168:     exceeded = []
L169:     for member, exp in zip(team, expenses):
L170:         budget = budgets[member["level"]]
L171:         total = sum(e["amount"] for e in exp)
L172:         if total > budget["travel_limit"]:
L173:             exceeded.append({
L174:                 "name": member["name"],
L175:                 "spent": total,
L176:                 "limit": budget["travel_limit"]
L177:             })
L178: 
L179:     print(json.dumps(exceeded))`
L180: Copy
L181: 
L182: Claude's context receives only the final result: the two to three people who exceeded their budget. The 2,000+ line items, the intermediate sums, and the budget lookups do not affect Claude’s context, reducing consumption from 200KB of raw expense data to just 1KB of results.
L183: 
L184: The efficiency gains are substantial:
L185:   * Token savings: By keeping intermediate results out of Claude's context, PTC dramatically reduces token consumption. Average usage dropped from 43,588 to 27,297 tokens, a 37% reduction on complex research tasks.
L186:   * Reduced latency: Each API round-trip requires model inference (hundreds of milliseconds to seconds). When Claude orchestrates 20+ tool calls in a single code block, you eliminate 19+ inference passes. The API handles tool execution without returning to the model each time.
L187:   * Improved accuracy: By writing explicit orchestration logic, Claude makes fewer errors than when juggling multiple tool results in natural language. Internal knowledge retrieval improved from 25.6% to 28.5%; cite12†GIA benchmarks†arxiv.org from 46.5% to 51.2%.
L188: Production workflows involve messy data, conditional logic, and operations that need to scale. Programmatic Tool Calling lets Claude handle that complexity programmatically while keeping its focus on actionable results rather than raw data processing.
L189: ### How Programmatic Tool Calling works
L190: #### 1. Mark tools as callable from code
L191: Add code_execution to tools, and set allowed_callers to opt-in tools for programmatic execution:
L192: 
L193:     `{
L194:       "tools": [
L195:         {
L196:           "type": "code_execution_20250825",
L197:           "name": "code_execution"
L198:         },
L199:         {
L200:           "name": "get_team_members",
L201:           "description": "Get all members of a department...",
L202:           "input_schema": {...},
L203:           "allowed_callers": ["code_execution_20250825"] # opt-in to programmatic tool calling
L204:         },
L205:         {
L206:           "name": "get_expenses",
L207:      	...
L208:         },
L209:         {
L210:           "name": "get_budget_by_level",
L211:     	...
L212:         }
L213:       ]
L214:     }`
L215: Copy
L216: 
L217: The API converts these tool definitions into Python functions that Claude can call.
L218: #### 2. Claude writes orchestration code
L219: 
L220: Instead of requesting tools one at a time, Claude generates Python code:
L221: 
L222:     `{
L223:       "type": "server_tool_use",
L224:       "id": "srvtoolu_abc",
L225:       "name": "code_execution",
L226:       "input": {
L227:         "code": "team = get_team_members('engineering')\n..." # the code example above
L228:       }
L229:     }`
L230: 
L231: Copy
L232: #### 3. Tools execute without hitting Claude's context
L233: 
L234: When the code calls get_expenses(), you receive a tool request with a caller field:
L235: 
L236:     `{
L237:       "type": "tool_use",
L238:       "id": "toolu_xyz",
L239:       "name": "get_expenses",
L240:       "input": {"user_id": "emp_123", "quarter": "Q3"},
L241:       "caller": {
L242:         "type": "code_execution_20250825",
L243:         "tool_id": "srvtoolu_abc"
L244:       }
L245:     }`
L246: 
L247: Copy
L248: You provide the result, which is processed in the Code Execution environment rather than Claude's context. This request-response cycle repeats for each tool call in the code.
L249: #### 4. Only final output enters context
L250: 
L251: When the code finishes running, only the results of the code are returned to Claude:
L252: 
L253:     `{
L254:       "type": "code_execution_tool_result",
L255:       "tool_use_id": "srvtoolu_abc",
L256:       "content": {
L257:         "stdout": "[{\"name\": \"Alice\", \"spent\": 12500, \"limit\": 10000}...]"
L258:       }
L259:     }`
L260: 
L261: Copy
L262: 
L263: This is all Claude sees, not the 2000+ expense line items processed along the way.
L264: ### When to use Programmatic Tool Calling
L265: 
L266: Programmatic Tool Calling adds a code execution step to your workflow. This extra overhead pays off when the token savings, latency improvements, and accuracy gains are substantial.
L267: 
L268: Most beneficial when:
L269:   * Processing large datasets where you only need aggregates or summaries
L270:   * Running multi-step workflows with three or more dependent tool calls
L271:   * Filtering, sorting, or transforming tool results before Claude sees them
L272:   * Handling tasks where intermediate data shouldn't influence Claude's reasoning
L273:   * Running parallel operations across many items (checking 50 endpoints, for example)
L274: 
L275: Less beneficial when:
L276:   * Making simple single-tool invocations
L277:   * Working on tasks where Claude should see and reason about all intermediate results
L278:   * Running quick lookups with small responses
L279: ## Tool Use Examples
L280: ### The challenge
L281: 
L282: JSON Schema excels at defining structure–types, required fields, allowed enums–but it can't express usage patterns: when to include optional parameters, which combinations make sense, or what conventions your API expects.
L283: Consider a support ticket API:
L284: 
L285:     `{
L286:       "name": "create_ticket",
L287:       "input_schema": {
L288:         "properties": {
L289:           "title": {"type": "string"},
L290:           "priority": {"enum": ["low", "medium", "high", "critical"]},
L291:           "labels": {"type": "array", "items": {"type": "string"}},
L292:           "reporter": {
L293:             "type": "object",
L294:             "properties": {
L295:               "id": {"type": "string"},
L296:               "name": {"type": "string"},
L297:               "contact": {
L298:                 "type": "object",
L299:                 "properties": {
L300:                   "email": {"type": "string"},
L301:                   "phone": {"type": "string"}
L302:                 }
L303:               }
L304:             }
L305:           },
L306:           "due_date": {"type": "string"},
L307:           "escalation": {
L308:             "type": "object",
L309:             "properties": {
L310:               "level": {"type": "integer"},
L311:               "notify_manager": {"type": "boolean"},
L312:               "sla_hours": {"type": "integer"}
L313:             }
L314:           }
L315:         },
L316:         "required": ["title"]
L317:       }
L318:     }`
L319: Copy
L320: 
L321: The schema defines what's valid, but leaves critical questions unanswered:
L322: 
L323:   * Format ambiguity: Should `due_date` use "2024-11-06", "Nov 6, 2024", or "2024-11-06T00:00:00Z"?
L324:   * ID conventions: Is `reporter.id` a UUID, "USR-12345", or just "12345"?
L325:   * Nested structure usage: When should Claude populate `reporter.contact`?
L326:   * Parameter correlations: How do `escalation.level` and `escalation.sla_hours` relate to priority?
L327: These ambiguities can lead to malformed tool calls and inconsistent parameter usage.
L328: ### Our solution
L329: Tool Use Examples let you provide sample tool calls directly in your tool definitions. Instead of relying on schema alone, you show Claude concrete usage patterns:
L330: 
L331:     `{
L332:         "name": "create_ticket",
L333:         "input_schema": { /* same schema as above */ },
L334:         "input_examples": [
L335:           {
L336:             "title": "Login page returns 500 error",
L337:             "priority": "critical",
L338:             "labels": ["bug", "authentication", "production"],
L339:             "reporter": {
L340:               "id": "USR-12345",
L341:               "name": "Jane Smith",
L342:               "contact": {
L343:                 "email": "jane@acme.com",
L344:                 "phone": "+1-555-0123"
L345:               }
L346:             },
L347:             "due_date": "2024-11-06",
L348:             "escalation": {
L349:               "level": 2,
L350:               "notify_manager": true,
L351:               "sla_hours": 4
L352:             }
L353:           },
L354:           {
L355:             "title": "Add dark mode support",
L356:             "labels": ["feature-request", "ui"],
L357:             "reporter": {
L358:               "id": "USR-67890",
L359:               "name": "Alex Chen"
L360:             }
L361:           },
L362:           {
L363:             "title": "Update API documentation"
L364:           }
L365:         ]
L366:       }`
L367: Copy
L368: 
L369: From these three examples, Claude learns:
L370: 
L371:   * Format conventions: Dates use YYYY-MM-DD, user IDs follow USR-XXXXX, labels use kebab-case
L372:   * Nested structure patterns: How to construct the reporter object with its nested contact object
L373:   * Optional parameter correlations: Critical bugs have full contact info + escalation with tight SLAs; feature requests have reporter but no contact/escalation; internal tasks have title only
L374: In our own internal testing, tool use examples improved accuracy from 72% to 90% on complex parameter handling.
L375: ### When to use Tool Use Examples
L376: 
L377: Tool Use Examples add tokens to your tool definitions, so they’re most valuable when accuracy improvements outweigh the additional cost.
L378: 
L379: Most beneficial when:
L380: 
L381:   * Complex nested structures where valid JSON doesn't imply correct usage
L382:   * Tools with many optional parameters and inclusion patterns matter
L383:   * APIs with domain-specific conventions not captured in schemas
L384:   * Similar tools where examples clarify which one to use (e.g., `create_ticket` vs `create_incident`)
L385: Less beneficial when:
L386: 
L387:   * Simple single-parameter tools with obvious usage
L388:   * Standard formats like URLs or emails that Claude already understands
L389:   * Validation concerns better handled by JSON Schema constraints
L390: ## Best practices
L391: 
L392: Building agents that take real-world actions means handling scale, complexity, and precision simultaneously. These three features work together to solve different bottlenecks in tool use workflows. Here's how to combine them effectively.
L393: ### Layer features strategically
L394: 
L395: Not every agent needs to use all three features for a given task. Start with your biggest bottleneck:
L396: 
L397:   * Context bloat from tool definitions → Tool Search Tool
L398:   * Large intermediate results polluting context → Programmatic Tool Calling
L399:   * Parameter errors and malformed calls → Tool Use Examples
L400: 
L401: This focused approach lets you address the specific constraint limiting your agent's performance, rather than adding complexity upfront.
L402: Then layer additional features as needed. They're complementary: Tool Search Tool ensures the right tools are found, Programmatic Tool Calling ensures efficient execution, and Tool Use Examples ensure correct invocation.
L403: ### Set up Tool Search Tool for better discovery
L404: 
L405: Tool search matches against names and descriptions, so clear, descriptive definitions improve discovery accuracy.
L406: 
L407:     `// Good
L408:     {
L409:         "name": "search_customer_orders",
L410:         "description": "Search for customer orders by date range, status, or total amount. Returns order details including items, shipping, and payment info."
L411:     }
L412: 
L413:     // Bad
L414:     {
L415:         "name": "query_db_orders",
L416:         "description": "Execute order query"
L417:     }`
L418: 
L419: Copy
L420: Add system prompt guidance so Claude knows what's available:
L421: 
L422:     `You have access to tools for Slack messaging, Google Drive file management,
L423:     Jira ticket tracking, and GitHub repository operations. Use the tool search
L424:     to find specific capabilities.`
L425: 
L426: Copy
L427: 
L428: Keep your three to five most-used tools always loaded, defer the rest. This balances immediate access for common operations with on-demand discovery for everything else.
L429: ### Set up Programmatic Tool Calling for correct execution
L430: Since Claude writes code to parse tool outputs, document return formats clearly. This helps Claude write correct parsing logic:
L431: 
L432:     `{
L433:         "name": "get_orders",
L434:         "description": "Retrieve orders for a customer.
L435:     Returns:
L436:         List of order objects, each containing:
L437:         - id (str): Order identifier
L438:         - total (float): Order total in USD
L439:         - status (str): One of 'pending', 'shipped', 'delivered'
L440:         - items (list): Array of {sku, quantity, price}
L441:         - created_at (str): ISO 8601 timestamp"
L442:     }`
L443: Copy
L444: 
L445: See below for opt-in tools that benefit from programmatic orchestration:
L446: 
L447:   * Tools that can run in parallel (independent operations)
L448:   * Operations safe to retry (idempotent)
L449: ### Set up Tool Use Examples for parameter accuracy
L450: 
L451: Craft examples for behavioral clarity:
L452: 
L453:   * Use realistic data (real city names, plausible prices, not "string" or "value")
L454:   * Show variety with minimal, partial, and full specification patterns
L455:   * Keep it concise: 1-5 examples per tool
L456:   * Focus on ambiguity (only add examples where correct usage isn't obvious from schema)

L161: ## Evaluating Claude Opus 4.5
L162: 
L163: We give prospective performance engineering candidates a notoriously difficult take-home exam. We also test new models on this exam as an internal benchmark. Within our prescribed 2-hour time limit, Claude Opus 4.5 scored higher than any human candidate ever^{1}.
L164: The take-home test is designed to assess technical ability and judgment under time pressure. It doesn’t test for other crucial skills candidates may possess, like collaboration, communication, or the instincts that develop over years. But this result—where an AI model outperforms strong candidates on important technical skills—raises questions about how AI will change engineering as a profession.
L165: Our cite32†Societal Impacts and cite33†Economic Futures research is aimed at understanding these kinds of changes across many fields. We plan to share more results soon.
L166: Software engineering isn’t the only area on which Claude Opus 4.5 has improved. Capabilities are higher across the board—Opus 4.5 has better vision, reasoning, and mathematics skills than its predecessors, and it is state-of-the-art in many domains:^{2}
L167: 
L168: cite34†Image: Comparison table showing frontier model performance across popular benchmarks L169: 
L170: SWE-bench Multilingual Aider Polyglot BrowseComp-Plus Vending-Bench
L171: cite35†Image Opus 4.5 writes better code, leading across 7 out of 8 programming languages on SWE-bench Multilingual.
L172: 
L173: cite36†Image Opus 4.5 can solve challenging coding problems with ease with a 10.6% jump over Sonnet 4.5 on Aider Polyglot.
L174: 
L175: cite37†Image Opus 4.5 improves on frontier agentic search with a significant jump on BrowseComp-Plus.
L176: 
L177: cite38†Image Opus 4.5 stays on track over the long haul earning 29% more than Sonnet 4.5 on Vending-Bench.
L178: The model’s capabilities outpace some of the benchmarks we use in our tests. A common benchmark for agentic capabilities is cite39†τ2-bench†github.com , which measures the performance of agents in real-world, multi-turn tasks. In one scenario, models have to act as an airline service agent helping a distressed customer. The benchmark expects models to refuse a modification to a basic economy booking since the airline doesn’t allow changes to that class of tickets.
L179: Instead, Opus 4.5 found an insightful (and legitimate) way to solve the problem: upgrade the cabin first, then modify the flights.
L180: 
L181:     `Let me think about what options I have within my policy:
L182: 
L183:     1. Modify flights - Basic economy cannot be modified. This is clear in the policy.
L184:     2. Change cabin - Wait, let me check this option! The policy says:
L185:     "In other cases, all reservations, including basic economy, can change cabin without changing the flights."
L186: 
L187:     But he wants to change the flights, not just the cabin. However, what if we:
L188:     - Change the cabin first (which IS allowed for basic economy), then
L189:     - Change the flights (which is allowed for non-basic economy)
L190: 
L191:     So the strategy could be:
L192:     1. Upgrade his cabin from basic economy to economy (or business)
L193:     2. Then modify the flights to be 2 days later
L194: 
L195:     This would cost more money, but it’s a legitimate path within the policy!`
L196: Copy
L197: 
L198: The benchmark technically scored this as a failure because Claude’s way of helping the customer was unanticipated. But this kind of creative problem solving is exactly what we’ve heard about from our testers and customers—it’s what makes Claude Opus 4.5 feel like a meaningful step forward.
L199: In other contexts, finding clever paths around intended constraints could count as reward hacking—where models “game” rules or objectives in unintended ways. Preventing such misalignment is one of the objectives of our safety testing, discussed in the next section.
L200: ## A step forward on safety
L201: 
L202: As we state in our cite40†system card , Claude Opus 4.5 is the most robustly aligned model we have released to date and, we suspect, the best-aligned frontier model by any developer. It continues our trend towards safer and more secure models:
L203: 
L204: cite41†Image In our evaluation, “concerning behavior” scores measure a very wide range of misaligned behavior, including both cooperation with human misuse and undesirable actions that the model takes at its own initiative [3].
L205: Our customers often use Claude for critical tasks. They want to be assured that, in the face of malicious attacks by hackers and cybercriminals, Claude has the training and the “street smarts” to avoid trouble. With Opus 4.5, we’ve made substantial progress in robustness against prompt injection attacks, which smuggle in deceptive instructions to fool the model into harmful behavior. Opus 4.5 is harder to trick with prompt injection than any other frontier model in the industry:
L206: cite42†Image Note that this benchmark includes only very strong prompt injection attacks. It was developed and run by cite43†Gray Swan†www.grayswan.ai .
L207: 
L208: You can find a detailed description of all our capability and safety evaluations in the cite40†Claude Opus 4.5 system card .
L209: ## New on the Claude Developer Platform
L210: 
L211: As models get smarter, they can solve problems in fewer steps: less backtracking, less redundant exploration, less verbose reasoning. Claude Opus 4.5 uses dramatically fewer tokens than its predecessors to reach similar or better outcomes.
L212: But different tasks call for different tradeoffs. Sometimes developers want a model to keep thinking about a problem; sometimes they want something more nimble. With our new effort parameter on the Claude API, you can decide to minimize time and spend or maximize capability.
L213: Set to a medium effort level, Opus 4.5 matches Sonnet 4.5’s best score on SWE-bench Verified, but uses 76% fewer output tokens. At its highest effort level, Opus 4.5 exceeds Sonnet 4.5 performance by 4.3 percentage points—while using 48% fewer tokens.
L214:

L220: ## Product updates
L221: 
L222: Products like Claude Code show what’s possible when the kinds of upgrades we’ve made to the Claude Developer Platform come together. Claude Code gains two upgrades with Opus 4.5. L223: Claude Code is also now cite50†available in our desktop app†claude.ai , letting you run multiple local and remote sessions in parallel: perhaps one agent fixes bugs, another researches GitHub, and a third updates docs.
L224: For cite51†Claude app†www.claude.com users, long conversations no longer hit a wall—Claude automatically summarizes earlier context as needed, so you can keep the chat going. cite52†Claude for Chrome†claude.ai , which lets Claude handle tasks across your browser tabs, is now available to all Max users.
